Source of truth for the story: X:/Claude-Skills/kip-site/debrief-kit/README.md. Pattern: cms/topicweave/release.json + docs/topicweave-release.md.

fieldData.summary: kip turns the rotation of people raising a newborn into one team. Its site is one page with a 3D house you can step into: every room shows one feature, and every phone in it works.
fieldData.objective-cadet: Babies aren’t raised by one tired parent. They’re raised by a rotation: two parents, a grandparent, a nanny, a night doula. kip puts them all in one shared log, with the face of whoever logged each feed, nap, diaper and dose. The old site explained that across twelve pages. The new one is a house: tap a room and you’re inside one feature, watching June’s village use it. Grandpa gets the shift handoff at the door, Nana saves the first smile in the living room, kip catches a second vitamin D dose in the kitchen, the nursery dims for the 3am feed, and the study builds the report for Dr. Patel. Every phone in the house works. It’s a [[Test flight]]: a concept with no app yet, and the site says so.
fieldData.objective-engineer: One page, coded by hand after an ideation board and wireframes in Figma. The house is a Spline scene: eight characters and a dog built from simple shapes with their own expressions, five rooms with a camera move each, a night mode for the nursery and 88 objects that react when tapped. The page owns everything the scene can’t do from inside its embed (the phones, the sounds, the mute button) and reads what happens in the house through Spline variables. Chrome’s WebGPU path dropped parts of the scene on Windows, so the viewer is forced onto WebGL. On phones the house becomes a wide card with room buttons, tested live on an Android phone, and the scene went from about 2 million polygons to 0.75 million with no visible change.

fieldData.name: A house you can step into
fieldData.cadet: Tap a room and the camera glides in beside it, the other rooms dim, the people inside react, and that room’s phone slides in on the open side.
fieldData.why: A list of five features is easy to skim past. Walking into the room where a feature happens, with the people it happens to, is hard to forget.
fieldData.engineer: Each room has its own camera target and the side its phone docks on, so the room always sits beside the phone, never under it. Veils dim the other rooms edge to edge, and the camera keeps a small lean toward the cursor, never a full orbit.

fieldData.name: Night for the nursery
fieldData.cadet: Open the nursery and the whole scene turns to night: the sky darkens, the moon and stars rise, the yard dims and the attic window glows. Leave and the day comes back.
fieldData.why: 3am mode is a feeling more than a feature. Turning the lights down on the whole house says it before anyone reads a word.
fieldData.engineer: One room state drives everything: the open room picks the sound, the phone and the speech bubbles, and the nursery swaps the yard and house colors to their night set. The night switch is pre-warmed so it doesn’t stutter the first time.

fieldData.name: A 3D scene that behaves like a website
fieldData.cadet: The house is a 3D scene, but the phones, sounds and mute button belong to the page, so it scrolls, loads and behaves like the rest of the site.
fieldData.why: An embedded 3D scene usually lives in its own box and ignores the page around it. Here the page and the house work as one.
fieldData.engineer: The embed’s HTML layer sat over the canvas and swallowed every tap, and it couldn’t send messages out. So the layer is click-through, the page owns the phones and the audio, and the scene reports the open room and each sound through Spline variables the page reads. The viewer is forced onto WebGL, because Chrome’s WebGPU path dropped the sky, roof and walls on Windows.

fieldData.name: Poke anything
fieldData.cadet: Coats swing, blocks hop, the crib mobile turns, a tree sways and a robin flies off, and Biscuit wags. 88 things in the house react when you tap them.
fieldData.why: People explore a house by touching things. Every small reaction rewards curiosity and keeps them in the room long enough to see the feature.
fieldData.engineer: Every object has its own tap sensor, and one table maps each name to a small effect (hop, swing, wiggle, squash, spin, a door on its hinge). Tapping an object also opens its room, so curiosity always lands on a feature.

fieldData.name: Phones get their own house
fieldData.cadet: On a phone the house is a wide card with a button for each room, and the app phone sits below it like a sheet.
fieldData.why: A full-screen 3D scene on a tall screen made the house tiny. On a phone people need big targets and the feature right under their thumb.
fieldData.engineer: Tested live on an Android phone: the tall canvas lost, so phones get a wide card, room buttons inside it and the dock as a bottom sheet sized to half the screen. Because the card moves as you scroll, the page re-measures the canvas so taps land where you aim.

fieldData.name: The village, built from shapes
fieldData.cadet: Eight people and a dog, each built from simple shapes, with mixed skin tones and a different eye color each. They blink, smile, look surprised or get sleepy, and light up when tapped.
fieldData.why: A log with a face on every entry only works if the faces are easy to tell apart, and a village should look like a real one.
fieldData.engineer: Every character shares one face rig (eyes, brows, mouth and a set of expressions on a loop), so a new character is a new look, not new code. Each was reviewed on its own: Sam’s collar took three tries, and June moved to a round baby body. The same 3D faces are the avatars inside the app phones.

fieldData.name: One log instead of a group chat
fieldData.problem: With five people caring for one baby, the group chat becomes the log, and nobody trusts it.
fieldData.fix: One shared log where every feed, nap and diaper carries the face of whoever logged it.
fieldData.result: “Who fed her last?” gets answered by opening the app, not by texting everyone.
fieldData.engineer: Every entry has one shape (who, what, when), so the log, the handoff and the counts read from the same list.

fieldData.name: Shift changes without lost details
fieldData.problem: Every shift change loses something: the last feed time, the nap that ran long, the note about the rash.
fieldData.fix: When someone comes in, kip sums up everything since they left, with a note from the parents. One tap and June’s theirs.
fieldData.result: Grandpa starts caught up, without a phone call or a note on the fridge.
fieldData.engineer: In the house it’s the Entry: Ari hands June to Grandpa, and his phone shows the summary before he asks.

fieldData.name: No double doses
fieldData.problem: Two caregivers each give the morning vitamin D, because neither knew the other already had.
fieldData.fix: Before logging a med, kip shows who already logged it today and asks first.
fieldData.result: A second dose takes a deliberate “Log it anyway”, not a habit.
fieldData.engineer: In the kitchen the sheet opens on its own when Rosa logs: Ari’s 9:02 entry, Don’t log it, or Log it anyway, which flags the entry.

fieldData.name: A product you can walk through
fieldData.problem: The first kip site explained the product across twelve pages, so seeing all of it meant a lot of clicking and reading.
fieldData.fix: One page with a house where every room demonstrates one feature, with a working phone in each.
fieldData.result: The whole product in one scroll, and every feature is something you do, not something you read.
fieldData.engineer: The house grows from a card to full screen as you scroll, then five sections tell the same features again with the same tappable phone.

fieldData.name: A concept that doesn’t pretend
fieldData.problem: A concept site dressed up as an app-store listing promises an app that doesn’t exist.
fieldData.fix: No reviews or users. The store buttons explain there’s nothing in the stores yet, and the early-access form says it sends nothing.
fieldData.result: The site can be shown to anyone without a caveat, because it never claims more than it is.
fieldData.engineer: Nothing you tap is saved, and the footer says June and her village are made up.
